items.stem: Which of the following best describes "DNA ligase"?
options: A change in the base sequence of a gene
An agent that increases the rate of mutation, such as UV radiation, X-rays or certain chemicals
The tRNA carrying methionine with anticodon UAC that binds to the start codon in the P site to begin translation
An enzyme that joins DNA fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds between adjacent nucleotides
items.answer: An enzyme that joins DNA fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds between adjacent nucleotides
items.markingKey: D. "DNA ligase" is an enzyme that joins DNA fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds between adjacent nucleotides.

items.stem: Why is replication described as semi-conservative?
options: Each new molecule has one parental strand and one new strand.
Only half the DNA is copied.
items.answer: Each new molecule has one parental strand and one new strand.
items.markingKey: A. One old, one new.

items.stem: Distinguish between the leading strand and the lagging strand.
items.answer: The leading strand is synthesised continuously towards the replication fork; the lagging strand is synthesised away from the fork in short Okazaki fragments joined by DNA ligase.
items.markingKey: The leading strand is synthesised continuously towards the replication fork; the lagging strand is synthesised away from the fork in short Okazaki fragments joined by DNA ligase. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: After one generation in ¹⁴N medium, DNA from bacteria previously grown in ¹⁵N formed a single band of intermediate density. Which model was ruled out?
items.answer: conservative replication
items.markingKey: A. Conservative would give a heavy and a light band.

items.stem: A student claims: "In replication, one double helix is entirely old and the other entirely new." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: This is the conservative model, which Meselson and Stahl disproved; each new helix has one old and one new strand.
items.markingKey: This is the conservative model, which Meselson and Stahl disproved; each new helix has one old and one new strand. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
A DNA sample was cut with a restriction enzyme and separated by gel electrophoresis alongside a DNA ladder. The distances moved from the well are shown.

Ladder fragment / bp | Distance moved / mm
5000 | 20.4
3000 | 24.6
2000 | 27.9
1000 | 33.5
500 | 39.1
250 | 44.7

Unknown fragment X moved 27.8 mm.

(a) State which ladder fragments X lies between. [1]
(b) Distance moved is proportional to log₁₀(fragment size). Use the ladder to estimate the size of X. [3]
(c) Explain why DNA fragments move through the gel. [2]
(d) Explain why fragments of different sizes separate. [1]
items.answer: (a) between 3000 and 2000 bp (b) about 2015 bp (accept ±10 %) (c) DNA has negatively charged phosphate groups and is attracted to the positive electrode. (d) Smaller fragments move more easily through the pores of the gel, so they travel further in a given time.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] Correct pair (A1). (b) [3] Plot/use distance vs log size (M1); read off log size 3.30 (M1); ≈ 2015 bp (A1). (c) [2] Negative charge (A1); move to anode (A1). (d) [1] Size/gel resistance (A1).

items.stem: Outline the stages of PCR and explain how PCR and gel electrophoresis are used together in DNA profiling.
items.answer: Denaturation 95 °C; annealing 55 °C; extension 72 °C; Taq; doubling per cycle; STR loci; electrophoresis; charge and size; ladder; comparison; uses in forensics and paternity.
items.markingKey: Denaturation 95 °C; annealing 55 °C; extension 72 °C; Taq; doubling per cycle; STR loci; electrophoresis; charge and size; ladder; comparison; uses in forensics and paternity.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "DNA profiling evidence alone should be enough to convict a suspect."
items.answer: DNA profiling is powerful evidence but should be considered with other evidence, as it shows presence rather than guilt.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: STR profiles at many loci give very low random-match probabilities; it has also freed wrongly convicted people. Arguments against: contamination or transfer can place innocent DNA at a scene; presence of DNA does not prove a person committed the crime; relatives share profiles. Supported judgement: DNA profiling is powerful evidence but should be considered with other evidence, as it shows presence rather than guilt. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "Okazaki fragments".
items.answer: Short sections of DNA synthesised discontinuously on the lagging strand during replication, later joined by DNA ligase
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: short sections of DNA synthesised discontinuously on the lagging strand during replication, later joined by DNA ligase. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how the Meselson–Stahl experiment supported semi-conservative replication.
items.answer: E. coli grown in ¹⁵N medium so DNA heavy; transferred to ¹⁴N; DNA extracted and centrifuged in CsCl density gradient; after one generation one intermediate band (rules out conservative); after two generations intermediate and light bands (rules out dispersive).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: E. coli grown in ¹⁵N medium so DNA heavy; transferred to ¹⁴N; DNA extracted and centrifuged in CsCl density gradient; after one generation one intermediate band (rules out conservative); after two generations intermediate and light bands (rules out dispersive). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Kwame writes: "DNA polymerase can start a new strand without a primer." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to an existing 3′ end, so a primer is needed.
items.markingKey: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to an existing 3′ end, so a primer is needed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: E. coli with only ¹⁵N DNA were transferred to ¹⁴N medium and allowed to replicate for 5 generations. What fraction of DNA molecules is hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N)?
items.markingKey: B. After 5 generations there are 2^5 = 32 molecules; only the 2 containing an original strand are hybrid: 2/32 = 1/16.

items.stem:
Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli for many generations in medium containing ¹⁵N, then transferred them to medium containing only ¹⁴N. Samples were taken after each generation, DNA was extracted and centrifuged in a caesium chloride density gradient. The positions of bands were recorded.

Generations in ¹⁴N | Heavy (¹⁵N/¹⁵N) band | Intermediate band | Light (¹⁴N/¹⁴N) band
0 | present | absent | absent
1 | absent | present | absent
2 | absent | present | present
3 | absent | ? | ?

(a) State the result after one generation in ¹⁴N. [1]
(b) Explain how the result after one generation rules out conservative replication. [2]
(c) Explain how the result after two generations rules out dispersive replication. [2]
items.answer: (a) A single intermediate band only. (b) Conservative replication would give one heavy and one light band; only an intermediate band was seen, so each molecule contained heavy and light DNA. (c) Dispersive replication would give a single band of lighter-than-intermediate density; two bands (intermediate and light) were seen.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] Intermediate band only (A1). (b) [2] Prediction of conservative model (A1); comparison (R1). (c) [2] Prediction of dispersive model (A1); comparison (R1).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "DNA profiling evidence alone should be enough to convict a suspect."
items.answer: DNA profiling is powerful evidence but should be considered with other evidence, as it shows presence rather than guilt.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: STR profiles at many loci give very low random-match probabilities; it has also freed wrongly convicted people. Arguments against: contamination or transfer can place innocent DNA at a scene; presence of DNA does not prove a person committed the crime; relatives share profiles. Supported judgement: DNA profiling is powerful evidence but should be considered with other evidence, as it shows presence rather than guilt.

items.stem: Which are the three stop codons?
items.answer: UAA, UAG and UGA
items.markingKey: UAA, UAG and UGA. They code for no amino acid.

items.stem: Explain the difference between translation and transcription.
items.answer: Transcription makes mRNA from a DNA template using RNA polymerase in the nucleus; translation makes a polypeptide from mRNA on ribosomes in the cytoplasm using tRNA.
items.markingKey: Transcription makes mRNA from a DNA template using RNA polymerase in the nucleus; translation makes a polypeptide from mRNA on ribosomes in the cytoplasm using tRNA. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why is degeneracy of the code an advantage?
options: Some base substitutions do not change the amino acid (silent mutations).
items.answer: Some base substitutions do not change the amino acid (silent mutations).
items.markingKey: B. Buffer against mutation.

items.stem: Using the deciphering of the genetic code by Nirenberg and Matthaei (1961) as an example, explain codons.
items.answer: Synthetic poly-U mRNA added to a cell-free system produced polyphenylalanine. This showed that UUU codes for phenylalanine and began the decoding of all 64 codons.
items.markingKey: Context (Synthetic poly-U mRNA added to a cell-free system produced polyphenylalanine.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: This showed that UUU codes for phenylalanine and began the decoding of all 64 codons. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to codons.

items.stem: Using the genetic code, which amino acid does the mRNA codon UCA code for?
items.answer: Ser
items.markingKey: A. UCA codes for Ser.

items.stem: A student claims: "Both strands of a gene are transcribed into mRNA." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Only the template strand is transcribed; the mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand (with U for T).
items.markingKey: Only the template strand is transcribed; the mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand (with U for T). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how the information in DNA is used to synthesise a polypeptide.
items.answer: Gene; RNA polymerase; promoter; template strand; complementary base pairing; mRNA leaves nucleus; ribosome; start codon AUG; tRNA anticodons; amino acids; peptide bonds; A, P, E sites; stop codon; degeneracy; universality.
items.markingKey: Gene; RNA polymerase; promoter; template strand; complementary base pairing; mRNA leaves nucleus; ribosome; start codon AUG; tRNA anticodons; amino acids; peptide bonds; A, P, E sites; stop codon; degeneracy; universality.

items.stem:
Yeast cells were exposed to different doses of ultraviolet (UV) radiation. The percentage surviving and the number of mutant colonies per 10⁶ surviving cells were recorded.

UV dose / J m⁻² | Survival / % | Mutants per 10⁶ survivors
0 | 100 | 4
10 | 77 | 26
20 | 60 | 47
40 | 34 | 90
80 | 14 | 175

(a) State the number of mutants per 10⁶ survivors at 20 J m⁻². [1]
(b) Calculate how many times greater the mutation frequency is at 40 J m⁻² than with no UV. [1]
(c) Describe the relationship between UV dose and mutation frequency. [2]
(d) Explain why mutants occur even with no UV. [1]
items.answer: (a) 47 (b) 22.5 times (c) Mutation frequency increases with dose, approximately linearly. (d) Spontaneous mutations arise from errors in DNA replication or natural background radiation/chemicals.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 47 (A1). (b) [1] 90/4 = 22.5 (A1). (c) [2] Positive (A1); linear/proportional (A1). (d) [1] Spontaneous/replication errors (A1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "RNA polymerase"?
options: The enzyme that separates DNA strands and links RNA nucleotides in the 5′ → 3′ direction during transcription
The DNA strand that is transcribed; the mRNA is complementary to it
A sequence of three bases on mRNA that codes for an amino acid or a stop signal
The enzyme that unwinds the double helix and separates the two strands by breaking hydrogen bonds between bases
items.answer: The enzyme that separates DNA strands and links RNA nucleotides in the 5′ → 3′ direction during transcription
items.markingKey: A. "RNA polymerase" is the enzyme that separates DNA strands and links RNA nucleotides in the 5′ → 3′ direction during transcription.

items.stem: Explain how the base sequence of a gene determines the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide.
items.answer: The base sequence of the template strand is transcribed into complementary mRNA; each triplet codon specifies one amino acid; tRNAs with complementary anticodons bring specific amino acids; the order of codons determines the order of amino acids.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The base sequence of the template strand is transcribed into complementary mRNA; each triplet codon specifies one amino acid; tRNAs with complementary anticodons bring specific amino acids; the order of codons determines the order of amino acids. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why can human insulin be produced by bacteria carrying the human gene?
options: The genetic code is universal, so bacterial ribosomes translate the codons into the same amino acids.
The code is different in bacteria.
items.answer: The genetic code is universal, so bacterial ribosomes translate the codons into the same amino acids.
items.markingKey: C. Universality.

items.stem:
A eukaryotic gene has five exons and four introns. The lengths are: exons 1–5: 204, 171, 213, 174, 162 nucleotides; introns: 455, 411, 1295, 1199 nucleotides. The exons present in the mature mRNA in three tissues are shown.

Tissue | Exons present | Mature mRNA coding length / nucleotides
liver | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 | 924
muscle | 1, 2, 4, 5 | ?
brain | 1, 3, 5 | 579

(a) State which exons are present in brain mRNA. [1]
(b) Calculate the coding length of the muscle mRNA. [1]
(c) Calculate the length of the primary transcript (pre-mRNA), excluding cap and tail. [1]
items.answer: (a) exons 1, 3 and 5 (b) 711 nucleotides (c) 4284 nucleotides
items.markingKey: (a) [1] Correct exons (A1). (b) [1] 204 + 171 + 174 + 162 = 711 (A1). (c) [1] Sum of all exons and introns = 4284 (A1).

items.stem: The template DNA strand reads 3′-TAC GGA CTT-5′. What is the mRNA sequence?
items.answer: 5′-AUG CCU GAA-3′
items.markingKey: C. Complementary, with U for T.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The genetic code is truly universal."
items.answer: The code is almost universal; small exceptions exist but do not undermine the evidence for common ancestry.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the same codons code for the same amino acids in bacteria, plants and animals; genes can be transferred between species and expressed. Arguments against: minor variations exist, e.g. in mitochondria and some protists (UGA codes for tryptophan). Supported judgement: The code is almost universal; small exceptions exist but do not undermine the evidence for common ancestry. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "initiator tRNA"?
options: A sequence of three bases on a tRNA molecule that pairs with a complementary codon on mRNA
Removal of introns from pre-mRNA and joining of exons, carried out by spliceosomes
DNA replication in which each new double helix contains one original (parental) strand and one newly synthesised strand
The tRNA carrying methionine with anticodon UAC that binds to the start codon in the P site to begin translation
items.answer: The tRNA carrying methionine with anticodon UAC that binds to the start codon in the P site to begin translation
items.markingKey: D. "initiator tRNA" is the tRNA carrying methionine with anticodon UAC that binds to the start codon in the P site to begin translation.

items.stem: Explain the post-transcriptional modification of eukaryotic pre-mRNA.
items.answer: A 5′ cap (methylated guanine) is added, protecting mRNA and aiding ribosome binding; a poly-A tail is added to the 3′ end, increasing stability; introns are removed by spliceosomes and exons joined; alternative splicing can produce different mRNAs; mature mRNA leaves via nuclear pores.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A 5′ cap (methylated guanine) is added, protecting mRNA and aiding ribosome binding; a poly-A tail is added to the 3′ end, increasing stability; introns are removed by spliceosomes and exons joined; alternative splicing can produce different mRNAs; mature mRNA leaves via nuclear pores. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why are proteins tagged with ubiquitin?
options: To mark them for breakdown by proteasomes.
To export them from the cell.
items.answer: To mark them for breakdown by proteasomes.
items.markingKey: A. Protein turnover.

items.stem: Maya writes: "Proteins are fully functional as soon as translation ends." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Many need post-translational modification such as cleavage, folding, glycosylation or phosphorylation.
items.markingKey: Many need post-translational modification such as cleavage, folding, glycosylation or phosphorylation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A eukaryotic gene contains 4 exons of lengths 189, 129, 279, 228 nucleotides and introns of 877, 627, 1060 nucleotides. Calculate the length of the pre-mRNA and of the spliced (coding) mRNA, and the percentage of the pre-mRNA removed.
items.answer: pre-mRNA 3389 nucleotides; mature 825 nucleotides; 76 % removed
items.markingKey: Sum of exons and introns = 3389 (A1); exons only = 825 (A1); 2564/3389 × 100 = 76 % (A1).

items.stem: Explain the modifications made to RNA and polypeptides after transcription and translation in eukaryotes.
items.answer: 5′ cap; poly-A tail; splicing by spliceosomes; alternative splicing; export from nucleus; initiation of translation; post-translational modification: cleavage (insulin), folding, disulfide bonds, glycosylation in Golgi; proteasome degradation.
items.markingKey: 5′ cap; poly-A tail; splicing by spliceosomes; alternative splicing; export from nucleus; initiation of translation; post-translational modification: cleavage (insulin), folding, disulfide bonds, glycosylation in Golgi; proteasome degradation.

items.stem: Which hormone is made as a precursor (preproinsulin) and cleaved to its active form?
items.answer: insulin
items.markingKey: C. Post-translational modification.

items.stem: Explain the difference between mature mRNA and pre-mRNA.
items.answer: Pre-mRNA is the primary transcript containing introns; mature mRNA has had introns removed and a 5′ cap and poly-A tail added.
items.markingKey: Pre-mRNA is the primary transcript containing introns; mature mRNA has had introns removed and a 5′ cap and poly-A tail added. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why is the first amino acid of most polypeptides methionine?
options: Translation starts at the codon AUG, which codes for methionine.
Methionine is attached to the 5′ cap.
Methionine is the smallest amino acid.
items.answer: Translation starts at the codon AUG, which codes for methionine.
items.markingKey: A. Start codon.

items.stem: A mutation at an intron–exon boundary prevents splicing. What is a likely result?
options: An intron is retained, changing the protein sequence or introducing a stop codon.
items.answer: An intron is retained, changing the protein sequence or introducing a stop codon.
items.markingKey: B. Splice-site mutation.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Introns are “junk DNA” with no function."
items.answer: Introns are not junk: they enable alternative splicing and regulation, although many intron sequences have no known specific function.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: introns are removed and not translated; they increase the energy cost of transcription. Arguments against: introns allow alternative splicing, increasing protein diversity; some contain regulatory sequences or code for small RNAs. Supported judgement: Introns are not junk: they enable alternative splicing and regulation, although many intron sequences have no known specific function. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "frameshift mutation"?
options: A mutation in which one base is replaced by another
The DNA strand that is transcribed; the mRNA is complementary to it
The enzyme that unwinds the double helix and separates the two strands by breaking hydrogen bonds between bases
An insertion or deletion of a number of bases that is not a multiple of three, changing every codon after the mutation
items.answer: An insertion or deletion of a number of bases that is not a multiple of three, changing every codon after the mutation
items.markingKey: D. "frameshift mutation" is an insertion or deletion of a number of bases that is not a multiple of three, changing every codon after the mutation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Mutations happen because an organism needs to adapt." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Mutations are random changes; selection then acts on them.
items.markingKey: Mutations are random changes; selection then acts on them. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why can a mutation in a somatic cell cause cancer but not be inherited?
options: It is passed to daughter cells by mitosis but not to gametes.
items.answer: It is passed to daughter cells by mitosis but not to gametes.
items.markingKey: B. Somatic vs germ-line.

items.stem: The mRNA 5′-AUG UCA AAC GUA GGU AUU UGA-3′ undergoes a mutation: insertion of U after base 4. Use the genetic code to give the original and the mutant amino acid sequences and explain the effect.
items.answer: original Met–Ser–Asn–Val–Gly–Ile–STOP; mutant Met–Phe–Lys–Arg–Arg–Tyr–Leu; frameshift alters all codons after the mutation
items.markingKey: Original translated (A1); mutant codons re-read in new frame (A1); frameshift explanation – all downstream codons change, may introduce early stop or remove stop (R1).

items.stem: A codon UGG (Trp) mutates to UGA. What type of mutation is this?
options: nonsense – it creates a stop codon
items.answer: nonsense – it creates a stop codon
items.markingKey: D. UGA is a stop codon.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Gene editing of human embryos should be permitted to prevent genetic disease."
items.answer: Somatic gene therapy is justified, but germ-line editing should remain restricted until safety and ethical issues are resolved.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: could eliminate serious inherited diseases such as Huntington’s; CRISPR is precise and increasingly reliable. Arguments against: off-target edits and mosaicism may cause harm to future generations; ethical concerns about consent, designer babies and inequality. Supported judgement: Somatic gene therapy is justified, but germ-line editing should remain restricted until safety and ethical issues are resolved.

items.stem: Which amino acid replaces glutamic acid in sickle-cell haemoglobin?
items.answer: valine
items.markingKey: B. GAG → GUG.

items.stem: Distinguish between nonsense mutations and missense mutations.
items.answer: Missense mutations change a codon so that a different amino acid is incorporated; nonsense mutations change a codon into a stop codon, ending translation early.
items.markingKey: Missense mutations change a codon so that a different amino acid is incorporated; nonsense mutations change a codon into a stop codon, ending translation early. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In an mRNA, the codon GUC (Val) mutates to UUC. Using the genetic code, classify this mutation.
items.answer: missense (different amino acid)
items.markingKey: B. UUC codes for Phe, so the mutation is missense (Val → Phe).

items.stem: Outline one way in which knockout mice shows gene knockout.
items.answer: Mice in which a specific gene has been inactivated are used to study gene function and model human diseases. The phenotype that results from the missing gene reveals its normal role.
items.markingKey: Context (Mice in which a specific gene has been inactivated are used to study gene function and model human diseases.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The phenotype that results from the missing gene reveals its normal role. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to gene knockout.

items.stem: Explain how gene knockout and CRISPR–Cas9 are used to study and change gene function.
items.answer: Knockout organisms; observing phenotype; CRISPR: guide RNA, Cas9, double-strand break, repair by NHEJ (knockout) or HDR (insertion); applications: research, crops, sickle-cell treatment; risks: off-target effects; conserved sequences.
items.markingKey: Knockout organisms; observing phenotype; CRISPR: guide RNA, Cas9, double-strand break, repair by NHEJ (knockout) or HDR (insertion); applications: research, crops, sickle-cell treatment; risks: off-target effects; conserved sequences.

items.stem: Which isotope did Meselson and Stahl use to label “heavy” DNA?
items.answer: nitrogen-15
items.markingKey: B. Bacteria grown on ¹⁵N medium.

items.stem: What type of bond joins amino acids in a polypeptide?
items.answer: peptide bond
items.markingKey: C. Formed by condensation on the ribosome.

items.stem: Which part of the ribosome first binds to the mRNA?
items.answer: the small subunit
items.markingKey: the small subunit. Binds near the 5′ cap and scans to AUG.

items.stem: Explain how CRISPR–Cas9 can be used to edit genes.
items.answer: A guide RNA complementary to the target sequence is made; it binds Cas9 and guides it to the target in the genome; Cas9 cuts both strands; the cell repairs the cut, often introducing errors (knockout), or a supplied template is inserted by homology-directed repair, editing the gene.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A guide RNA complementary to the target sequence is made; it binds Cas9 and guides it to the target in the genome; Cas9 cuts both strands; the cell repairs the cut, often introducing errors (knockout), or a supplied template is inserted by homology-directed repair, editing the gene. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why is a heat-stable polymerase needed in PCR?
options: The reaction is repeatedly heated to 95 °C, which would denature most enzymes.
It works faster at low temperatures.
items.answer: The reaction is repeatedly heated to 95 °C, which would denature most enzymes.
items.markingKey: A. Taq polymerase.

items.stem: Arjun writes: "Both strands of a gene are transcribed into mRNA." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Only the template strand is transcribed; the mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand (with U for T).
items.markingKey: Only the template strand is transcribed; the mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand (with U for T). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why are introns removed before translation?
options: They are non-coding; including them would change the amino acid sequence.
items.answer: They are non-coding; including them would change the amino acid sequence.
items.markingKey: C. Splicing.

items.stem: Explain the consequences of insertions and deletions in a gene.
items.answer: Insertion or deletion of a number of bases not a multiple of three shifts the reading frame; all downstream codons change; often a premature stop codon arises; the polypeptide is non-functional; deletion of three bases removes one amino acid (e.g. cystic fibrosis ΔF508).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Insertion or deletion of a number of bases not a multiple of three shifts the reading frame; all downstream codons change; often a premature stop codon arises; the polypeptide is non-functional; deletion of three bases removes one amino acid (e.g. cystic fibrosis ΔF508). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between DNA replication in cells and PCR.
items.answer: Replication in cells uses helicase to separate strands and many enzymes (primase, ligase) at body temperature; PCR uses heat to separate strands, synthetic primers and Taq polymerase, and copies only a target sequence.
items.markingKey: Replication in cells uses helicase to separate strands and many enzymes (primase, ligase) at body temperature; PCR uses heat to separate strands, synthetic primers and Taq polymerase, and copies only a target sequence. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Use the genetic code to give the amino acid sequence coded by this mRNA: 5′-AUG ACA CCG CUA UCU CGA UGA-3′
items.answer: Met–Thr–Pro–Leu–Ser–Arg
items.markingKey: Codons read in triplets from AUG: AUG = Met, ACA = Thr, CCG = Pro, CUA = Leu, UCU = Ser, CGA = Arg, UGA = STOP (A2 for all correct; A1 for one error).

items.stem: A gene has exons of 210, 150 and 330 nucleotides and two introns of 800 nucleotides each. How long is the mature mRNA coding region?
items.answer: 690 nucleotides

items.stem: Deletion of three consecutive bases within a gene usually causes:
options: a frameshift of all later codons
loss of one amino acid without a frameshift
items.answer: loss of one amino acid without a frameshift
items.markingKey: C. A whole codon removed, e.g. ΔF508 in cystic fibrosis.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Meselson–Stahl experiment (1958) and explain what it reveals about semi-conservative replication.
items.answer: E. coli moved from ¹⁵N to ¹⁴N medium gave one intermediate band after one generation, then intermediate and light bands. Each new molecule contained one heavy parental strand and one light new strand.
items.markingKey: Context (E. coli moved from ¹⁵N to ¹⁴N medium gave one intermediate band after one generation, then intermediate and light bands.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Each new molecule contained one heavy parental strand and one light new strand. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to semi-conservative replication.

items.stem: The coding region of an mRNA, from the start codon to the stop codon inclusive, is 456 nucleotides long. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide, and how many tRNA molecules bind (assuming one per amino acid)?
items.answer: 151 amino acids; 151 tRNAs
items.markingKey: 456/3 = 152 codons (M1); stop codon codes for no amino acid → 151 (A1).

items.stem: With reference to alternative splicing of the Dscam gene in Drosophila, explain how it illustrates alternative splicing.
items.answer: One gene can potentially produce over 38 000 different mRNAs through alternative splicing. Different combinations of exons give a huge diversity of proteins from a single gene, used in neurone recognition.
items.markingKey: Context (One gene can potentially produce over 38 000 different mRNAs through alternative splicing.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Different combinations of exons give a huge diversity of proteins from a single gene, used in neurone recognition. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to alternative splicing.

items.stem:
Yeast cells were exposed to different doses of ultraviolet (UV) radiation. The percentage surviving and the number of mutant colonies per 10⁶ surviving cells were recorded.

UV dose / J m⁻² | Survival / % | Mutants per 10⁶ survivors
0 | 100 | 3
10 | 79 | 28
20 | 59 | 53
40 | 34 | 102
80 | 11 | 201

(a) State the number of mutants per 10⁶ survivors at 20 J m⁻². [1]
(b) Calculate how many times greater the mutation frequency is at 40 J m⁻² than with no UV. [1]
(c) Describe the relationship between UV dose and mutation frequency. [2]
items.answer: (a) 53 (b) 34.0 times (c) Mutation frequency increases with dose, approximately linearly.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 53 (A1). (b) [1] 102/3 = 34.0 (A1). (c) [2] Positive (A1); linear/proportional (A1).

items.stem:
A DNA sample was cut with a restriction enzyme and separated by gel electrophoresis alongside a DNA ladder. The distances moved from the well are shown.

Ladder fragment / bp | Distance moved / mm
5000 | 20.8
3000 | 25.0
2000 | 28.3
1000 | 34.0
500 | 39.7
250 | 45.4

Unknown fragment X moved 27.5 mm.

(a) State which ladder fragments X lies between. [1]
(b) Distance moved is proportional to log₁₀(fragment size). Use the ladder to estimate the size of X. [3]
(c) Explain why DNA fragments move through the gel. [2]
items.answer: (a) between 3000 and 2000 bp (b) about 2215 bp (accept ±10 %) (c) DNA has negatively charged phosphate groups and is attracted to the positive electrode.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] Correct pair (A1). (b) [3] Plot/use distance vs log size (M1); read off log size 3.35 (M1); ≈ 2215 bp (A1). (c) [2] Negative charge (A1); move to anode (A1).

items.stem: "The genetic code is truly universal." Discuss.
items.answer: The code is almost universal; small exceptions exist but do not undermine the evidence for common ancestry.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the same codons code for the same amino acids in bacteria, plants and animals; genes can be transferred between species and expressed. Arguments against: minor variations exist, e.g. in mitochondria and some protists (UGA codes for tryptophan). Supported judgement: The code is almost universal; small exceptions exist but do not undermine the evidence for common ancestry. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem:
A eukaryotic gene has five exons and four introns. The lengths are: exons 1–5: 270, 267, 171, 255, 144 nucleotides; introns: 700, 459, 615, 1344 nucleotides. The exons present in the mature mRNA in three tissues are shown.

Tissue | Exons present | Mature mRNA coding length / nucleotides
liver | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 | 1107
muscle | 1, 2, 4, 5 | ?
brain | 1, 3, 5 | 585

(a) State which exons are present in brain mRNA. [1]
(b) Calculate the coding length of the muscle mRNA. [1]
(c) Calculate the length of the primary transcript (pre-mRNA), excluding cap and tail. [1]
(d) Calculate the maximum number of amino acids coded by the liver mRNA, assuming the stop codon is the last codon of exon 5. [2]
items.answer: (a) exons 1, 3 and 5 (b) 936 nucleotides (c) 4225 nucleotides (d) 368
items.markingKey: (a) [1] Correct exons (A1). (b) [1] 270 + 267 + 255 + 144 = 936 (A1). (c) [1] Sum of all exons and introns = 4225 (A1). (d) [2] 1107/3 = 369 codons (M1); minus stop = 368 (A1).

items.stem: "Gene editing of human embryos should be permitted to prevent genetic disease." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Somatic gene therapy is justified, but germ-line editing should remain restricted until safety and ethical issues are resolved.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: could eliminate serious inherited diseases such as Huntington’s; CRISPR is precise and increasingly reliable. Arguments against: off-target edits and mosaicism may cause harm to future generations; ethical concerns about consent, designer babies and inequality. Supported judgement: Somatic gene therapy is justified, but germ-line editing should remain restricted until safety and ethical issues are resolved. Markbands (8 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The enzyme that adds nucleotides to a growing DNA strand in the 5′ → 3′ direction, using the other strand as a template"?
items.answer: DNA polymerase
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of DNA polymerase.

items.stem: Define the term "transcription".
items.answer: The synthesis of RNA using a DNA strand as a template, catalysed by RNA polymerase
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the synthesis of RNA using a DNA strand as a template, catalysed by RNA polymerase. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "poly-A tail".
items.answer: A chain of adenine nucleotides added to the 3′ end of pre-mRNA that increases its stability
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a chain of adenine nucleotides added to the 3′ end of pre-mRNA that increases its stability. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between germ-line mutations and somatic mutations.
items.answer: Germ-line mutations occur in cells that produce gametes and can be inherited; somatic mutations occur in body cells, are passed only to daughter cells and may cause cancer but are not inherited.
items.markingKey: Germ-line mutations occur in cells that produce gametes and can be inherited; somatic mutations occur in body cells, are passed only to daughter cells and may cause cancer but are not inherited. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the process of DNA replication.
items.answer: Helicase unwinds the helix and breaks hydrogen bonds; each strand acts as a template; free nucleotides pair with complementary bases (A–T, C–G); DNA polymerase links nucleotides 5′ → 3′ by phosphodiester bonds; leading strand continuous, lagging strand in Okazaki fragments joined by ligase; result: two identical molecules, each semi-conservative.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Helicase unwinds the helix and breaks hydrogen bonds; each strand acts as a template; free nucleotides pair with complementary bases (A–T, C–G); DNA polymerase links nucleotides 5′ → 3′ by phosphodiester bonds; leading strand continuous, lagging strand in Okazaki fragments joined by ligase; result: two identical molecules, each semi-conservative. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between anticodons and codons.
items.answer: Codons are base triplets on mRNA; anticodons are complementary base triplets on tRNA that pair with codons.
items.markingKey: Codons are base triplets on mRNA; anticodons are complementary base triplets on tRNA that pair with codons. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between mature mRNA and pre-mRNA.
items.answer: Pre-mRNA is the primary transcript containing introns; mature mRNA has had introns removed and a 5′ cap and poly-A tail added.
items.markingKey: Pre-mRNA is the primary transcript containing introns; mature mRNA has had introns removed and a 5′ cap and poly-A tail added. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why do many base substitutions have no effect on the protein?
options: The genetic code is degenerate, so the new codon may code for the same amino acid.
items.answer: The genetic code is degenerate, so the new codon may code for the same amino acid.
items.markingKey: A. Silent mutations.

items.stem: Explain the difference between DNA replication in cells and PCR.
items.answer: Replication in cells uses helicase to separate strands and many enzymes (primase, ligase) at body temperature; PCR uses heat to separate strands, synthetic primers and Taq polymerase, and copies only a target sequence.
items.markingKey: Replication in cells uses helicase to separate strands and many enzymes (primase, ligase) at body temperature; PCR uses heat to separate strands, synthetic primers and Taq polymerase, and copies only a target sequence. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Use the genetic code to give the amino acid sequence coded by this mRNA: 5′-AUG UUU AAU UCU GGC UGA-3′
items.answer: Met–Phe–Asn–Ser–Gly
items.markingKey: Codons read in triplets from AUG: AUG = Met, UUU = Phe, AAU = Asn, UCU = Ser, GGC = Gly, UGA = STOP (A2 for all correct; A1 for one error).

items.stem: A mutation removes the poly-A signal from a gene. What is the likely effect?
options: The mRNA is less stable and is degraded faster, so less protein is made.
items.answer: The mRNA is less stable and is degraded faster, so less protein is made.
items.markingKey: B. Poly-A tail stabilises mRNA.

items.stem: With reference to sickle-cell anaemia, explain how it illustrates the effects of a base substitution.
items.answer: A single base substitution in the β-globin gene changes Glu to Val and causes sickling of red blood cells. One amino acid change alters haemoglobin properties and causes disease, while heterozygotes are more resistant to malaria.
items.markingKey: Context (A single base substitution in the β-globin gene changes Glu to Val and causes sickling of red blood cells.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: One amino acid change alters haemoglobin properties and causes disease, while heterozygotes are more resistant to malaria. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the effects of a base substitution.

items.stem: A PCR reaction starts with 50 copies of a target DNA sequence. Assuming perfect doubling, calculate the number of copies after 25 cycles. If each cycle takes 4 minutes, how long does the PCR take?
items.answer: 1.68e+09 copies; 100 minutes

items.stem: A tRNA carries an anticodon 3′-CAU-5′. Which amino acid does it carry?
items.answer: Val
items.markingKey: B. The anticodon pairs with codon 5′-GUA-3′, which codes for Val.

items.stem: Proinsulin has 86 amino acids; insulin has 51. What happened?
options: A section (C-peptide) was removed by cleavage after translation.
items.answer: A section (C-peptide) was removed by cleavage after translation.
items.markingKey: A. Post-translational modification.

items.stem: A student claims: "All mutations are harmful." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Most are neutral; some are harmful and a few are beneficial, providing variation for evolution.
items.markingKey: Most are neutral; some are harmful and a few are beneficial, providing variation for evolution. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "DNA profiling evidence alone should be enough to convict a suspect."
items.answer: DNA profiling is powerful evidence but should be considered with other evidence, as it shows presence rather than guilt.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: STR profiles at many loci give very low random-match probabilities; it has also freed wrongly convicted people. Arguments against: contamination or transfer can place innocent DNA at a scene; presence of DNA does not prove a person committed the crime; relatives share profiles. Supported judgement: DNA profiling is powerful evidence but should be considered with other evidence, as it shows presence rather than guilt.

items.stem: Describe the features of the genetic code and explain their significance.
items.answer: Triplet; 64 codons; degenerate; universal; non-overlapping; start and stop codons; significance: mutations may be silent, gene transfer between species possible, evidence of common ancestry.
items.markingKey: Triplet; 64 codons; degenerate; universal; non-overlapping; start and stop codons; significance: mutations may be silent, gene transfer between species possible, evidence of common ancestry.

items.stem:
Yeast cells were exposed to different doses of ultraviolet (UV) radiation. The percentage surviving and the number of mutant colonies per 10⁶ surviving cells were recorded.

UV dose / J m⁻² | Survival / % | Mutants per 10⁶ survivors
0 | 100 | 2
10 | 78 | 29
20 | 63 | 56
40 | 34 | 109
80 | 11 | 215

(a) State the number of mutants per 10⁶ survivors at 20 J m⁻². [1]
(b) Calculate how many times greater the mutation frequency is at 40 J m⁻² than with no UV. [1]
(c) Describe the relationship between UV dose and mutation frequency. [2]
(d) Explain why mutants occur even with no UV. [1]
(e) Explain how UV causes mutations. [2]
(f) Explain why survival decreases at high doses. [2]
(g) Suggest why human skin cancer risk increases with sun exposure. [1]
(h) Explain why mutation frequency is expressed per 10⁶ surviving cells. [2]
items.answer: (a) 56 (b) 54.5 times (c) Mutation frequency increases with dose, approximately linearly. (d) Spontaneous mutations arise from errors in DNA replication or natural background radiation/chemicals. (e) UV is absorbed by DNA bases, forming thymine dimers between adjacent pyrimidines; errors during repair or replication cause base changes. (f) More DNA damage, including in essential genes; cells cannot repair it, so they die or cannot divide. (g) UV causes mutations in skin cells, including in genes controlling cell division (oncogenes/tumour suppressors), leading to uncontrolled division. (h) Many cells are killed at higher doses, so expressing mutants per survivor allows a fair comparison of mutation rate between doses.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 56 (A1). (b) [1] 109/2 = 54.5 (A1). (c) [2] Positive (A1); linear/proportional (A1). (d) [1] Spontaneous/replication errors (A1). (e) [2] Absorbed by bases/thymine dimers (A1); replication/repair errors (A1). (f) [2] Damage to essential genes (A1); cell death (A1). (g) [1] Mutation in cell-cycle genes (A1). (h) [2] Survival differs between doses (A1); fair comparison (A1).
